newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels enter diamond hub as peace talks set.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels enter diamond hub as peace talks set.

text.p: Rebels marched into the diamond mining capital of Mbuji-Mayi in their latest advance in Zaire on Friday, a day before peace talks between government and rebel representatives were to start in South Africa.
"We understand rebel forces have entered the town. It is in the process of changing hands," said a mining source who had been in radio contact with the town.

Traders in the second city Lubumbashi, also targeted by the rebels, said colleagues in Mbuji-Mayi confirmed the advance by the rebels, whose leader Laurent Kabila is demanding that President Mobutu Sese Seko step down.
"The rebels broadcast on local radio, saying 'We have liberated the town, you have nothing to fear, stay at home'," one said.

Another said the rebels spread the same message with loudhailers in the streets. He said most Zairean troops who had been in the town appeared to have fled westward in stolen vehicles after looting shops and diamond traders' premises.

The Tutsi-dominated rebels have already overrun the east of Zaire since they intensified their campaign in October to unseat Mobutu. They now control about one quarter of Africa's third largest country.
As in many previous takeovers, there were no reports of fighting in Mbuji-Mayi although shooting was heard overnight.

Troops stole vehicles from the state-owned La Miniere de Bakwanga (MIBA) diamond mining company and looted diamond dealers' businesses before fleeing towards the town of Kananga, about 100 km (62 miles) to the west, expatriate sources said.
Rebels have been slowly encircling Lubumbashi, Zaire's copper mining hub, which they say is their next target.
Reports of continued rebel advances in the mining regions of central Zaire and political confusion in Zaire's capital Kinshasa had earlier made the peace talks appear in doubt.
But South Africa's Foreign Affairs Ministry said on Friday talks would go ahead in Pretoria on Saturday between representatives of the Zairean government and the rebels.
The South African statement said the talks would start at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Saturday at the government's main headquarters, the Union Buildings, in Pretoria.
In South Africa Kabila's negotiators said Mobutu's team did not appear to be serious about talks and indicated they would leave if discussions did not begin without delay.
"There are procedures we must follow. They cannot expect us to jump on things," a Zairean government official said.

In Kinshasa, Mobutu's allies began moves to oust opposition stalwart Etienne Tshisekedi for excluding them from power in his first act since becoming prime minister at head of a government that hopes to end the civil war.

Diplomats said the controversy triggered by Tshisekedi's appointment -- and his offer of six key cabinet posts to rebels -- had complicated the situation. The rebels have shown open contempt for politicians who served Mobutu's 31-year rule and rejected the cabinet offer.
Mobutu himself refused to be drawn into the political crisis stirred by Tshisekedi, telling reporters on Friday in Kinshasa this was not the business of the head of state.

Tshisekedi made enemies even among his supporters in parliament on Thursday by dissolving the transitional assembly, dominated by Mobutu supporters. Leaders of the pro-Mobutu FPC parliamentary majority called urgent talks on Friday with the pro-Tshisekedi members to agree strategy on ousting him.

"We have not ousted Tshisekedi. He has ousted himself," FPC vice-president Mutombo Bakafu Asenda told Reuters in Kinshasa. "We do not recognise that there is a prime minister...we cannot apply the rules of the constitution to maintain a prime minister who does not himself recognise the constitution."
